dp-01.a.text: A credit model sees a wave of applicants from a new region. For any given income, employment and history profile, default rates are exactly what the model expects.
dp-01.a.why: The inputs moved into new territory but the rule is intact, so predictions hold wherever the training data covered these profiles. The thing to watch is thinly covered regions, where the model is extrapolating; a new rule is not needed.
dp-01.b.text: A credit model sees the same wave of applicants from a new region. For an identical income, employment and history profile, default rates there are twice what the model expects.
dp-01.b.why: Identical inputs now produce different outcomes, so P(Y|X) has changed. No amount of rebalancing the input mix will fix a relationship that no longer holds.

dp-02.a.text: A pricing model's error jumps on a Tuesday. Investigation finds a competitor launched an aggressive discount campaign that morning.
dp-02.a.why: A real change in the world altered the relationship the model encodes. Retraining on post-change data is the correct response.
dp-02.b.text: A pricing model's error jumps on a Tuesday. Investigation finds the overnight ETL job began writing list price into the field that previously held net price.
dp-02.b.why: Nothing about pricing behaviour changed — the model is being fed a different quantity under the same name. Retraining here bakes the defect in and hides it.

dp-03.a.text: Over six months a fraud model degrades as an old attack pattern is progressively replaced by a new one. Throughout the period, both patterns arrive in volume.
dp-03.a.why: Two distinct concepts overlapping in time, with the mixture weight moving. An ensemble that keeps a model per concept handles this well.
dp-03.b.text: Over six months a fraud model degrades as attackers continuously adjust transaction sizes upward in small steps, with no distinct old and new pattern at any point.
dp-03.b.why: One concept moving smoothly through intermediate states. A rolling retraining window tracks it; concept-switching machinery has nothing to switch between.

dp-04.a.text: A screening model is deployed at a new clinic. The patients are younger and fitter than the training population, and disease prevalence is unchanged.
dp-04.a.why: The feature distribution moved while the outcome mix did not. The concern is extrapolation into thinly-covered input regions.
dp-04.b.text: A screening model is deployed at a new clinic. The patients look demographically identical to the training population, but disease prevalence is a quarter of what it was.
dp-04.b.why: P(Y) moved with P(X|Y) intact, so the model's ranking still works but its probabilities are systematically too high. Prior correction, not retraining.

dp-05.a.text: A collections model's share of high-risk scores rises from 12% to 25% in a month. Outcomes take ninety days to observe, so none are yet available for this cohort.
dp-05.a.why: An output-distribution change with no labels is a signal to investigate, not a finding. It may be a correct response to a genuinely riskier population.
dp-05.b.text: A collections model's share of high-risk scores rises from 12% to 25% in a month, and the cohort from ninety days ago has now resolved with precision down 18 points.
dp-05.b.why: Labels have arrived and quality has actually fallen. Only now is retraining justified on evidence rather than on the shape of a histogram.

dp-06.a.text: A logistics model's accuracy collapses every year in the fortnight before Christmas and recovers immediately afterwards.
dp-06.a.why: A known concept that comes back on a cycle. Retire nothing: keep the seasonal model and select it by context.
dp-06.b.text: A logistics model's accuracy collapses in the fortnight after a permanent change to national delivery regulations, and never recovers.
dp-06.b.why: An abrupt, one-way change with no return. The pre-change model has no further use and the pre-change data has limited value for retraining.

dp-07.a.text: A moderation team rewrites its guidance so that a category of borderline content is now labelled 'violating' where it was previously 'acceptable'. The content arriving is unchanged.
dp-07.a.why: Same inputs, different labels: the mapping was redefined. Every historical label under the old guidance is now partly wrong for training purposes.
dp-07.b.text: A moderation team's guidance is unchanged, but a viral trend means genuinely violating content rises from 2% to 9% of the queue.
dp-07.b.why: The rule is stable; the mix of outcomes moved. Thresholds and capacity planning need attention, not the model's learned boundary.

dp-08.a.text: Scores shift the day a new model version is released. A fixed reference sample, replayed through both versions, reproduces the shift exactly.
dp-08.a.why: Identical inputs producing different outputs isolates the change to the model. This is the expected use of a golden reference sample at release.
dp-08.b.text: Scores shift the day a new model version is released. The same fixed reference sample, replayed through both versions, produces identical outputs.
dp-08.b.why: If the model is provably unchanged on fixed inputs, the live inputs must have changed — and a same-day coincidence points at the deploy's data-side changes, not at the world.
